How this edition is organised

Two parallel views of one dataset

  • Category-wise notes — the same passages regrouped by information type (definitions, classifications, causes, pathogenesis, morphology, clinical features, investigations, complications, comparisons, examination content…).
  • Book order — the untouched sequence, chapter by chapter and page by page, so the original textbook context is always recoverable.
  • Every card shows its source: volume, chapter number/title and printed page. Page chips jump straight into the book-order view at that page.
  • Passages that belong to several categories are listed in each of them; each card shows “also filed under” links.

Fidelity rules used by the builder

  • Every line of the Markdown is owned exactly once: inside a content block or recorded as a structural line (page anchor, separator, blank).
  • The build reconstructs the source byte-for-byte and compares SHA-256 hashes — see the completeness report.
  • OCR wording, spelling, symbols and garbled lines are preserved verbatim; nothing is silently corrected.
  • Category and subcategory labels are navigational aids only; they never replace the original text or its source data.

Fidelity statement

The source is an OCR extraction of photo-scanned pages. Its text contains scan noise, broken tables, misread characters and occasional page-header bleed. This edition deliberately keeps that text unchanged: no sentence was rewritten, no list item was removed, no figure caption was paraphrased, and no missing value was invented.

Reorganisation happens only at the level of labels and grouping: each passage is stored once, with its chapter, page and original heading, and the category views simply filter that one dataset. That is why the book-order view and every category view always agree word-for-word.

Uncertain OCR text is marked for review by being left exactly as printed. Periods, superscripts, fractions and table columns that the scanner merged are visible in the passage and should be cross-checked against the PDF when clinically important.

What was done, step by step

  1. Inventory. Parse the single-file edition into 57 merged chapters, 1,004 page anchors and one document-header record; capture each chapter's source PDF, printed page range and unit label.
  2. Segmentation. Split each page into passages at question starts, headings, list runs, table runs and page artefacts. A question passage runs from Q. to the next question and therefore contains its own Ans., answer text and (Ref: …) lines.
  3. Topic detection. Score every passage against the 31-category taxonomy using weighted phrases (headings weighted higher than body text), force-include categories whose signature phrase appears (e.g. “differential diagnosis”, “complications of”, “fate of”, “short note”, “Ref:”), add a chapter-topic prior, and keep up to five relevant categories per passage.
  4. Subcategory filing. Apply per-category phrase rules (gross vs microscopic, acute vs chronic, hematology vs oncology, etc.); the first matching subcategory wins, otherwise the category's general subcategory is used.
  5. Verification. Assign every source line to exactly one owner, rebuild the document from the owners, and compare SHA-256 hashes. Any unowned line fails the build.
  6. Rendering. Embed the single dataset once in this file. Category, book-order and search views all read the same records, so no view can drift from another.

Known limitations and review notes

  • OCR noise. The source is Tesseract output of photo-scans. Character confusions (e.g. Ca** for Ca²⁺, 10" for 10th edition, O, for O₂), merged words and broken columns are inherited unchanged. They are not corrected anywhere in this file.
  • Tables. Many printed tables were flattened by OCR into separate lines. Where the Markdown still contains pipe rows they render as tables; the rest remain line-by-line text, matching the source.
  • Category heuristics. Filing is phrase-based, not a human read of every sentence. A passage can be under-filed (e.g. a discussion of prognosis without the word “prognosis”) or over-filed (a passing mention). The primary category is the most reliable label; use search for exhaustive retrieval.
  • Subcategory defaults. When no subcategory phrase matches, the passage sits in the category's first/general subcategory. Subcategory counts are shown next to every filter so empty areas are obvious.
  • Page artefacts. 3,327 short passages are running headers, page numbers, separator rules or stray OCR glyphs. They are preserved under “Others → OCR page artefacts and running headers” rather than deleted.
  • Answer completeness follows the source. Some printed answers are genuinely one-line (“Please write from above”) or were lost in scanning; nothing was padded to fill the gap.
  • No clinical use. This is a study aid reproducing a copyrighted textbook for personal revision; verify anything clinically important against the original PDF.
